title: Hymn 3, sound: gagan mai thaal
hook: gagan mai thaal rav chand deepak bane (Dhanasri M1, ang 13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line was one sun: many seasons, one light. And this is a week's end. This week you met Sohila's first two hymns: the house of praise, the bride called, six schools, one sun. Today, hymn three. Day four hundred twenty-seven.
screen: `ONE SUN.` · `A WEEK: THE HOUSE, THE BRIDE, THE SIX, THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Some songs are famous far beyond the people who first sang them. Sohila's third hymn is one of those. It's sung in gurdwaras around the world, often in the evening, and musicians from outside the tradition have loved it too. If you've ever heard a long, slow Punjabi melody that opens on the word gagan, sky, you've probably heard it. It's by Guru Nanak, in Raag Dhanasri, on Ang 13. And it begins by looking straight up. Today: just the sound of the first line.
screen: `A HYMN SUNG AROUND THE WORLD.` → `IT OPENS ON ONE WORD: SKY.` → `GURU NANAK LOOKS UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening: gagan mai thaal, rav chand deepak bane. Word by word. Gagan: the sky, the whole vault of the heavens. Mai: in, or made of. Thaal: a platter, the round metal tray you'd carry food or offerings on. Rav: the sun. You met the sun yesterday as sooraj; rav is another old name for it. Chand: the moon. Deepak: lamps, the little flames set on a tray. Bane: have become. So: the sky is the platter, and the sun and moon have become its lamps. The line keeps going, and we'll open the rest tomorrow, but even this much is a whole picture. Somebody is holding a tray of light. The tray is the sky. The lamps are the two great lights we live by. Notice how the week has built to this. This week's first hymn began in a house. The second hymn walked through the six schools and ended at the sun. Now the third hymn takes the sun and moon and sets them on a platter, like an offering. Sohila keeps widening the frame: a doorway, a marketplace, the calendar, and now the whole sky. Notice the sounds too. Gagan, thaal, chand, deepak. The line moves in broad, open vowels, as if the mouth has to open wide to hold all that space. Say it and you'll feel it.
screen: `GAGAN: THE SKY.` · `THAAL: A PLATTER OF LIGHT.` · `RAV AND CHAND: SUN AND MOON.` · `DEEPAK: THE LAMPS.` · then, large: `GAGAN MAI THAAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the first line aloud. Gagan mai thaal, rav chand deepak bane. Say it once slowly, and let your mouth open fully on each long vowel: gaa-gan, thaal, chaand. Then say it again, and as you do, picture a round tray held up in both hands, with two flames on it. Now let the tray grow until it's the size of the sky. Rest in that picture and just breathe. If you pray, you can say the line once more at the end. The bell holds the time.
Hymn 3. Sohila's third hymn, by Guru Nanak in Raag Dhanasri: the sky is the platter, and the sun and moon have become its lamps.
Your line: gagan mai thaal. The sky is the platter. Tonight, if you can, step outside or to a window and look up for one full breath before you sleep. Day four hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn nightly as the third of Kirtan Sohila's five, and in many gurdwaras it is also sung on its own in the evening, often called the Aarti.

fork.setup: Guru Nanak looks up at the sky. what does the first line make of it?
options: a platter, with the sun and moon as its lamps.
an empty space with nothing in it.
fork.reveal: gagan mai thaal, rav chand deepak bane: the sky is a tray of offering, and sun and moon are its lamps.

original.note: Gurmukhi: gagan, the sky; the first word of Sohila's third hymn.

trapdoor: what you thought: gagan mai thaal is a line of nature poetry.
what it means: the sky is held up like a tray of offering, with the sun and moon as its lamps.
what a scholar hears: the hymn is in Raag Dhanasri on Ang 13; thaal and deepak are the platter and lamps used in a temple aarti.
